analysis.one_liner: Bans federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks, restricts gifts and sponsored seminars, and applies the judicial ethics code to the Supreme Court.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its June 2023 referral to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with no committee action, debate, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the ethics rules for the federal courts. It would bar federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks or businesses that could conflict with their cases, tighten the ban on gifts including free trips to privately sponsored judicial seminars, apply the judicial Code of Conduct to Supreme Court justices for the first time, create a complaint process and review committee for misconduct by justices, require judges to publicly list their conflicts, and stop courts from sealing information relevant to public health or safety. The bill was introduced in June 2023, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Litigants in federal court, who would get judges without personal financial stakes in the cases before them, public recusal lists, and live audio of appellate arguments. Court employees get anonymous workplace climate surveys covering harassment and discrimination. The public generally gets a transparent conflict-of-interest system for the judiciary, including the Supreme Court, plus a check on settlements and sealing orders that bury health and safety hazards revealed in lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who appears in federal court

how_it_helps.text: It bans federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning or trading individual stocks, bonds, hedge funds, derivatives, and closely held businesses, and bars them from corporate board seats — so a judge hearing a case cannot have money riding on the outcome. Judges could keep diversified index funds, government bonds, and their retirement plans.

It closes the 'personal hospitality' gift exception, counts paid travel, lodging, and meals as gifts, and directs the Judicial Conference to ban gifts connected to private judicial seminars — the all-expenses-paid education events that outside sponsors have long hosted for judges. It creates a taxpayer-funded Judicial Education Fund so judges can still attend approved seminars without a sponsor paying the way.

It applies the judicial Code of Conduct to Supreme Court justices, sets up a public complaint process for justice misconduct, and creates a Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee that can investigate complaints, refer potential crimes to the Justice Department, and send findings to the House Judiciary Committee for possible impeachment action.

It requires every judge to file a public list of interests and associations that would require recusal — including a spouse's financial interests — and requires written public explanations when a justice declines to step aside from a case.

It limits courts' ability to seal records and approve settlements that hide information relevant to public health or safety, and lets parties report hazards to federal and state regulators despite a settlement — so corporate misconduct documented in litigation cannot be buried by a confidentiality order.

It adds transparency measures aimed at ordinary court users: live online audio of appellate arguments, public case-assignment data, easier-to-use district court websites that clearly explain how to complain about a judge, and anonymous workplace climate surveys of court employees covering harassment and discrimination.

analysis.who_pays: Judges and justices who would have had to divest individual stocks, hedge-fund interests, and closely held businesses, and give up corporate board seats. Corporate sponsors of all-expenses-paid judicial seminars would lose their access channel. Companies defending health-and-safety cases would find it harder to seal records or keep settlements secret. Taxpayers would fund the Judicial Education Fund and the new review committee.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement of an ethics code on Supreme Court justices by Congress is constitutionally contested; critics argue judges discipline under Article III belongs to the courts themselves, and the bill addresses this only with a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that the Code of Conduct apply to the justices.

The bill creates a new Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee with subpoena-supported investigations, but conducts them largely in secret — complaints and committee information are barred from public disclosure unless a majority approves — which could limit the very transparency the bill aims for.

Judicial Conference advisory opinions on justice recusal petitions are nonbinding, so even under the bill a justice could publicly explain a decision to keep hearing a case without having to step aside.

The divestment mandate requires building a separate Federal Employee Investment Account system for judges, with new administrative costs authorized to be appropriated, and judges would have to restructure their finances to comply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but narrow: judges give up individual stock trading and sponsored junkets, and taxpayers fund a small judicial education fund (~$3 million a year) plus a new five-member review committee, in exchange for conflict-of-interest rules, a complaints process for the Supreme Court, and far more public information about recusals, speeches, and case assignments. The weakest parts are enforcement: the recusal advisory opinions for justices are nonbinding, the sense-of-Congress application of the ethics code is not enforceable on its own, and the review committee's strict confidentiality could keep complaint records from the public. The strongest parts — the stock ban, the gift clampdown, and the mandated public recusal lists — are straightforward and were left untouched because the bill never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced S. 1908 on June 8, 2023, joined by eight colleagues.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on June 8, 2023 — the same day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action in the roughly nineteen months remaining in the 118th Congress.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting federal judges and Supreme Court justices kept the existing self-policing system, their individual stock holdings, and their ability to accept sponsored trips; corporate sponsors of judicial seminars and companies that rely on sealed settlements were untouched as well.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Markey, Wyden, Smith, Merkley, Padilla, Cardin, and Sanders among the introducers).

against.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee held no hearing, no markup, and no vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; the bill never left the committee.

against.name: Supreme Court Justices
against.what_they_did: Responded to the 2023 ethics controversies by adopting their own voluntary code of conduct without an enforcement mechanism, rather than accepting binding outside rules of the kind this bill would impose.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with the Senate under Democratic control the bill still received no committee action.

industries.industry: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices (as a class of officeholders)
industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to hold individual stocks, accept sponsored trips, and police their own conduct without outside review, and subjects them to public complaint processes and fines up to $50,000 per violation. Sitting and retired judges kept all of these because the bill never moved.

industries.industry: Corporate and foundation sponsors of privately funded judicial seminars
industries.note: Sponsors pay for resort seminars where business-backed legal ideas are presented to judges whose courts they may appear before; the bill bans gifts connected to such seminars and forces sponsors to disclose their litigation activities. Nothing changed because the bill stalled.

The bill limits courts' willingness to seal records, approve confidential settlements, or enforce secrecy terms in cases involving public health or safety hazards, and protects whistleblowing to regulators. Companies currently use such confidentiality to keep documented hazards out of public view.
